anna.x:
On Sunday, the weather is warm and sunny. Leo knocks on Anna's door at ten o'clock.

"Do you want to see the best park in the city?" he asks.

"Yes, please!" says Anna. She puts on her shoes and takes her bag.

The park is not far. They walk along the river for fifteen minutes. There are a lot of people in the park. Some people are running. Some people are riding bikes. Children are playing on the grass, and an old man is feeding the ducks.

In the middle of the park, there is a small lake. Leo and Anna sit on a bench near the water. Leo buys two ice creams from a little café.

"Chocolate or strawberry?" he asks.

"Strawberry," says Anna. "Chocolate is your favourite, right?"

"How do you know?" Leo laughs.

"I'm a teacher," says Anna. "I notice things."

They sit and talk for a long time. Leo tells Anna about his job. He works in a music shop, and in the evenings he plays the guitar in a small café. Anna tells Leo about her school and her students. Her students are eight and nine years old. They are noisy, but they are very sweet.

"Do you like your new life here?" Leo asks.

Anna looks at the lake, the trees and the blue sky. "Yes," she says. "I really do."

On Wednesday, it rains all day. The sky is grey, and the streets are wet. Anna doesn't have an umbrella.

After school, she waits at the door. The rain is very heavy. "I can't walk home in this," she thinks.

Then she sees a small boy from her class. His name is Sam. He is standing next to her and looking at the rain too.

"Where is your mum, Sam?" Anna asks.

"She's late," says Sam. "She works in a hospital. Sometimes she's very late."

Anna smiles. "Then let's wait together. Do you like stories?"

"Yes!" says Sam.

They sit on a bench inside the school, and Anna tells him a story about a little robot who wanted to learn to read. Sam listens with big eyes. When the story ends, he asks, "Is it true?"

"Maybe," says Anna.

At six o'clock, Sam's mum runs in. Her coat is wet, and she looks tired. "I'm so sorry!" she says. "Thank you for waiting with him."

"It's no problem," says Anna. "Sam is a great listener."

Sam's mum has a big umbrella. "Where do you live?" she asks. "We can walk with you."

So the three of them walk home together under one umbrella. It is still raining, but Anna doesn't feel cold at all.

Anna's birthday is on Friday. She is twenty-six now. She doesn't tell anybody at work, because she is new and she feels shy.

In the morning, her mum calls her. "Happy birthday, my darling! Are you doing anything special today?"

"Not really," says Anna. "Maybe I'll buy a small cake."

At school, the day is normal. The children read, write and draw. But at the end of the last lesson, Sam stands up. "Miss Anna," he says, "close your eyes, please."

Anna is surprised, but she closes her eyes. She hears chairs and whispers and paper.

"Now open them!"

On her desk, there is a big card. It says HAPPY BIRTHDAY in red and green letters, and every child in the class has drawn a small picture on it. There are flowers, cats, a sun, a river and a little robot with blue eyes.

"How did you know?" Anna asks.

"My mum saw it on your bag," says Sam. Anna looks at her bag. Her old school name card is still on it, with her date of birth.

That evening, there is music outside her door again. Leo is standing there with his guitar, and Rosa from the shop is holding a cake with twenty-six candles.

"We heard it was a special day," says Rosa.

Anna laughs. She can't stop smiling. "Come in," she says. "Come in, everybody."

max.x:
One day, Mr. Green says, "Max, you have read every book in the workshop. Do you want to see more books?"

"More books?" says Max. His eyes blink green very fast. "Where?"

"In the library," says Mr. Green. "It is a big building full of books. Anyone can go there and read."

The library is in the centre of the town. Max rolls next to Mr. Green along the street. People look at the little robot and smile.

Inside, it is quiet and warm. There are shelves from the floor to the ceiling. Max has never seen so many books. There are books about the stars, books about the sea, books about animals and machines and far countries.

A young woman with glasses comes to them. "Hello! I'm Lily, the librarian. Can I help you?"

"My friend wants to read," says Mr. Green.

Lily looks at Max. "A robot who reads? That's wonderful! What do you like?"

Max thinks for a moment. "I like stories about small things that do big things," he says.

Lily laughs and brings him three books: a story about a brave ant, a story about a girl who builds a boat, and a book about the first airplane.

"You can take them home for two weeks," she says. "Then come back for more."

Max holds the books very carefully. "Thank you," he says. "This is the best place in the world."

After many weeks of reading, Max has a new idea. "Mr. Green," he says, "can a robot write a story?"

Mr. Green puts down his tools. "Why not? Every story starts with one sentence. Try it."

Max sits at the table. He takes a pencil in his small metal hand. He thinks and thinks. His eyes turn yellow, which means he is working hard.

Then he writes: "Once upon a time, there was a little robot who could not read."

He stops. "That's me," he says.

"Good stories often start with something true," says Mr. Green.

Max writes every evening. He writes about the workshop and the red book. He writes about the letters on the board and the night when he read the names of the shops. He writes about the library and Lily, and about all the brave little things in all the books.

After a month, his story is finished. It is twenty pages long. Max takes it to the library.

Lily reads it slowly. When she finishes, she is quiet for a moment. Then she says, "Max, can I put this on a shelf? I think other people will love it."

Today, if you visit the library in that town, you can find a small book with a blue cover. The title is The Robot Who Learned to Read. The author's name is Max.

light.x:
In the spring, the sea was calm and blue again. One morning, Tom saw a small boat coming towards the island. It was not the supply boat. It was a fishing boat, and its name was painted on the side: Sea Star.

The boat stopped at the little wooden pier. A young woman jumped out. She had dark hair and a red jacket, and she was carrying a basket.

"Are you the lighthouse keeper?" she asked.

"I am," said Tom. "Tom Harper."

"I'm Elena Ross. I wrote you a letter." She smiled and held out the basket. "My mother made this for you. Fresh bread, cheese and a cake. My father says the cake is the most important part."

Tom didn't know what to say. He had not had a visitor for a very long time. "Would you like some tea?" he asked at last.

They sat in the small kitchen. Pepper the cat jumped onto Elena's knees at once, which was very unusual. Elena asked about everything: the lamp, the stairs, the storms, the books on the shelf.

"Can I see the top of the tower?" she asked.

They climbed the hundred and twenty steps together. At the top, Elena looked out at the wide, shining sea. "So this is what you see every night," she said quietly.

"Every night," said Tom.

When she left, she promised to come back. And she did, almost every month, all through that summer.

One autumn day, a letter came from the town. Tom read it at the kitchen table. The lighthouse was going to be automatic. A computer would switch on the lamp every evening, and nobody would need to live on the island any more.

Tom folded the letter and looked out of the window for a long time.

On his last night, he climbed the hundred and twenty steps as he had done thousands of times before. He cleaned the glass, checked the machine and switched on the great lamp. The light began to turn, slowly, as it always did.

He stayed at the top all night. He watched the beam move across the dark water. He saw the lights of two ships far away, and he wondered who was on them and where they were going.

In the morning, the Sea Star came to the pier. Elena and her father helped him carry his boxes of books to the boat. Pepper sat in a basket and complained loudly.

"Where will you live now?" asked Elena.

"I've found a small house in the town," said Tom. "It has a window that looks at the sea. I can see the lighthouse from there."

The boat moved away from the island. Tom looked back at the white tower. It looked small now, and a little lonely.

"It will be all right," said Elena. "It still has a job to do."

"So do I," said Tom, and he was surprised to find that he was smiling. "So do I."

train.x:
Daniel stayed in Westport for a week. Every morning he sat with his grandmother, and every afternoon he walked along the sea front. He kept thinking about the woman on the train.

On the last day, he went to the small music school near the harbour. There was an old photograph in the hall: a group of children standing around a piano, and next to them a young teacher in a long coat. Under the photograph, someone had written: Miss M. Hale and her pupils, 1958.

Daniel looked at the picture for a long time. The teacher had the same soft expression he remembered from the train.

"Can I help you?" asked a man from the office.

"Miss Hale," said Daniel. "Does she still live in the town?"

The man looked surprised. "Margaret Hale? I'm sorry. She died many years ago. She was a wonderful teacher. Everyone here remembers her."

Daniel didn't explain. What could he say? He thanked the man and went outside. The sea was grey and quiet, and the wind smelled of salt.

That evening, on the train back to the city, he took out his phone and opened his calendar. Next to the words "visit home", it said, as always, "next month".

He deleted it. Then he wrote a new date, two weeks later, and under it he added: "Don't wait."

The train moved through the dark countryside. The seat opposite him was empty, but for a moment Daniel thought he could smell a light, old-fashioned perfume, like roses.

alice.x:
When Alice reached the shore, she was wet and tired, but she was still very small. She walked through a forest of tall grass until she came to a large mushroom. It was about the same height as she was.

She stood on her toes and looked over the edge of the mushroom. On the top sat a big blue Caterpillar. It was smoking a long pipe and taking no notice of her at all.

At last the Caterpillar took the pipe out of its mouth and looked at her. "Who are you?" it asked slowly.

"I hardly know, sir," said Alice. "I knew who I was when I got up this morning, but I have changed so many times since then."

"What do you mean by that?" said the Caterpillar. "Explain yourself!"

"I can't explain myself," said Alice, "because I'm not myself, you see. Being so many different sizes in one day is very confusing."

"It isn't," said the Caterpillar.

"Well, perhaps it isn't confusing for you," said Alice, "but when you turn into a butterfly one day, I think you will feel a little strange too."

The Caterpillar was quiet for a long time. Then it climbed down from the mushroom and began to crawl away into the grass. As it went, it said, "One side will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter."

"One side of what?" thought Alice.

"Of the mushroom," said the Caterpillar, as if she had asked aloud, and then it disappeared.

Alice broke off a piece from each side. She ate a tiny bit of the left piece, and then a tiny bit of the right, very carefully, until at last she was exactly her normal height again. "That's better," she said. "Now I must find that beautiful garden."

Soon Alice came to a little house in the forest. In front of it there was a long table under a tree, and three strange guests were having tea: a March Hare, a man in a very tall hat called the Hatter, and a sleepy little Dormouse, who was sitting between them with his eyes closed.

The table was very large, but the three of them were sitting together at one corner. "No room! No room!" they cried when they saw Alice coming.

"There's plenty of room!" said Alice, and she sat down in a big armchair at one end of the table.

"Have some juice," said the March Hare kindly.

Alice looked all round the table, but there was nothing on it except tea. "I don't see any juice," she said.

"There isn't any," said the March Hare.

"Then it wasn't very polite of you to offer it," said Alice angrily.

"It wasn't very polite of you to sit down without an invitation," said the March Hare.

The Hatter took a watch out of his pocket, shook it, and held it to his ear. "What day of the month is it?" he asked.

"The fourth," said Alice.

"Two days wrong!" said the Hatter sadly. "I told you butter wasn't good for watches!"

"It was the best butter," said the March Hare.

Alice soon learned that in this house it was always six o'clock, which meant it was always tea time. They never had time to wash the cups, so they simply moved round the table to clean ones.

After a while, Alice stood up. "That was the silliest tea-party I've ever been to!" she said, and she walked away into the forest. When she looked back, the Hatter and the March Hare were trying to put the Dormouse into the teapot.

Then she noticed a door in one of the trees. She went through it, and found herself once more in the long hall, close to the little glass table. This time she knew exactly what to do. She took the golden key, ate a small piece of mushroom, and at last she walked into the beautiful garden.
